quote: Fertig nicht definirt. Dieser Uebelstand wird schlimmer, je mehr man darüber nachdenkt
english: 'Finished' is not defined. This defect becomes worse the more one thinks about it.
topic: Reflecting on Cantor's letters, Hilbert considers the problem of which collections may be regarded as 'finished' (complete) in set theory, and proposes formulating set-theoretic propositions without the word 'set' and treating terms such as 'irrational number' merely as names for things with specified properties.

triage.modern_statement: This is a foundational problem, not a specific theorem. The question is what criterion decides which multiplicities count as 'finished' (fertige), i.e. consistent collections that may be treated as single objects or sets, and which are 'inconsistent' (absolutely infinite) multiplicities, such as the collection of all alephs or of all ordinals. In modern terms it asks for a precise, paradox-free criterion for set existence: the set versus proper class distinction, worked out by axiomatising set theory (limiting comprehension) rather than by Cantor's undefined notion of 'finished'. Hilbert's suggestion to drop the word 'set' and treat terms like 'irrational number' as names for things with stated properties fits his axiomatic, implicit-definition approach.
triage.answered_by: There is no single answer. The problem was dealt with by axiomatisation rather than by defining 'finished': Zermelo's 1908 axiomatisation of set theory, which restricts unlimited comprehension (Zermelo worked on this in Göttingen with Hilbert); Fraenkel and Skolem's additions that led to ZF/ZFC; and von Neumann's 1925 axiomatisation, later NBG (von Neumann–Bernays–Gödel), which makes the set versus proper class distinction explicit. Hilbert's own first response was his axiomatic treatment of the reals in 'Über den Zahlbegriff' (1900). This is not one of the 23 problems or the 24th problem. It is related in spirit to Problem 2, the consistency of arithmetic and analysis, but is not the same thing.

evidence.claim: Cantor wrote to Hilbert about 'fertige Mengen' in letters of 26 Sep 1897 and 6 Oct 1898, saying his work concerned finished sets and that theorems proved only for finished sets must not be applied to other multiplicities. This matches the context of the diary note.
In his letter to Dedekind of 28 July 1899, Cantor separated consistent multiplicities (sets) from inconsistent ones, prompted by the Burali-Forti contradiction about the multiplicity of all ordinals.

Hilbert dealt with these issues, including that the collection of all powers is an inconsistent ('unfinished') set, and looked for remedies such as the axiomatic approach of 'Über den Zahlbegriff' (1900).
Hilbert found his own paradox while struggling with Cantor's set theory. According to Hilbert, it led to Zermelo's version of the Zermelo–Russell paradox.
Zermelo's axioms restricted unlimited comprehension. Before that, his paradox was known only to Hilbert, Husserl and others in Göttingen.
NBG separates sets from proper classes, which are collections too large to be sets, such as the collection of all sets. This avoids the paradoxes.

triage.why: The note directly answers Cantor's 1897–1899 letters to Hilbert about 'fertige' versus inconsistent multiplicities. The problem it points to, that there is no definition of which collections are legitimate sets, was settled in practice by axiomatic set theory: Zermelo in 1908, ZF(C), and von Neumann/NBG, where proper classes play the role of Cantor's inconsistent multiplicities. Hilbert's idea of avoiding the word 'set' and treating mathematical terms as names for things with given properties matches his later axiomatic method. Questions about the nature of sets versus classes are still discussed in philosophy of set theory. But this particular defect is no longer an open mathematical research problem. My confidence is medium because the diary note is short and philosophical. Linking it to these later developments is a historical reading, not a claim made directly about this page in any source I found.
